n: This lecture is devoted to precursors. The topic: toluene, acetone, acetic anhydride, potassium permanganate, sulphuric and hydrochloric acids and the methods of their analysis. According to the outline, we review the definition of a precursor and its control, tables 18 and 19, preparation of the specimen for analysis, and then the properties, identity and assay of each substance. Key terms: precursor, the 1988 UN Convention, the control list, identification and the neutralisation method.

Precursors are substances that are included in the list, controlled in Uzbekistan, and used in the preparation of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. On the basis of the decisions of the 1988 UN Single Convention, 26 substances have been placed under international control as precursors. This section covers the analysis of toluene, acetone, acetic anhydride, potassium permanganate, and sulphuric and hydrochloric acids.

Legal basis. On 19 August 1999 the Law “On Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances” was adopted in the Republic of Uzbekistan. The law regulates social relations concerning the circulation of narcotic, intoxicating and precursor substances. It also requires strengthening of control over the production and supply of these substances. The scheme shows the sequence: in 1988 the UN single convention, 26 substances; on 19 August 1999 the law of the Republic of Uzbekistan; on 1 March 2001 the EU decision, on norephedrine.

The substances on the list are conventionally divided into two groups. The substances of group 1 make up the larger part of the formula. The substances of group 2 are considered auxiliary, but they too play a principal role. That is, both groups are important in preparing a narcotic drug.

International measures. On the basis of the decision of the European Union of 1 March 2001, measures for the production and control of norephedrine were strengthened in 15 countries. In 2001 the routes of sale of potassium permanganate in illicit international trade were identified and intercepted. In 2000, attempts by Colombia to export 20 tonnes of hydrochloric acid for the illicit production of cocaine were stopped.

Preparing the specimen for analysis. If the suspected substance is present in a small amount, its entire quantity must be submitted for laboratory analysis. From a powdered substance a few crystals are taken; if repeat analysis is required, twice the number of crystals is taken. A tablet, or a hard or soft narcotic substance, for example cannabis or opium, is first crushed with a spatula or a cutting tool.

The preparation procedure changes depending on the type of sample. A drug substance in capsules is carefully opened, and a small amount is taken and analysed. Plant raw materials are first crushed and then analysed; full analysis is carried out in laboratory conditions. For tobacco products, one pack of tobacco is opened, crushed, and then analysis is carried out.

t: Table 18: acetic anhydride, anthranilic acid derivatives
n: The first group in table 18. Acetic acid anhydride is used in preparing methaqualone and heroin. Anthranilic acid is a precursor of 4-methylaminorex and methaqualone. N-acetylanthranilic acid is indicated for methaqualone. In the table, beside each precursor, the product prepared from it is given.

Table 18, for the amphetamine group. 1-phenyl-2-propanone is the precursor of amphetamine, 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl-2-propanone of MDA and MDMA, and phenylacetic acid of MDA and its derivatives. Isosafrole is used for methylenedioxyamphetamine, that is, MDA; safrole for MDEA; piperonal for amphetamine derivatives. Red phosphorus and pseudoephedrine are used in preparing pervitin.

Table 18, precursors for methcathinone and cathinone. Ephedrine, N-methylephedrine and potassium permanganate are used in preparing methcathinone. Norpseudoephedrine is considered the precursor of norcathinone, and phenylpropanolamine of cathinone and methcathinone.

Table 18, precursors for LSD and phencyclidine. Lysergic acid, ergometrine, that is, ergonovine, and ergotamine are used to prepare LSD. Piperidine, in turn, is the precursor of phencyclidine and tenocyclidine. In the table these pairs are shown in order.

Table 18 also lists solvents and reagents. Acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, that is, 2-butanone, toluene and diethyl ether are used as solvents in preparing many narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. Sulphuric and hydrochloric acids, apart from their salts, are used as reagents in preparing such substances. Acetone serves as a solvent in preparing pervitin, LSD, cocaine, heroin and others.

Table 19 shows the precursors as auxiliary substances. Starting substances: anthranilic acid, N-acetylanthranilic acid, isosafrole, lysergic acid, piperonal, piperidine, safrole, ergotamine, ephedrine and others. Reagents: acetic acid anhydride, red phosphorus, potassium permanganate, sulphuric and hydrochloric acids. Solvents: acetone, methyl ethyl ketone, that is, 2-butanone, toluene and diethyl ether.

t: Schemes for obtaining cocaine and heroin hydrochloride
n: In the textbook, the schemes for obtaining cocaine and heroin hydrochloride are given as figures. The example on the slide concerns heroin: morphine reacts with acetic anhydride, 250 l. Then, using acetone or ether 1500-2000 l and HCl 30 l, heroin hydrochloride is obtained; the yield is heroin HCl 100 kg. The scheme shows the sequence: opium, morphine, heroin, that is, diacetylmorphine, with acetic anhydride, then the hydrochloride with acetone, ether and HCl.

We summarise the precursors and the drugs prepared, by product. Acetic anhydride, anthranilic acid and N-acetylanthranilic acid are for methaqualone. Lysergic acid, ergometrine and ergotamine are for LSD. Ephedrine, N-methylephedrine and potassium permanganate are for methcathinone. Red phosphorus and pseudoephedrine are for pervitin. Piperidine is used for phencyclidine.

We compare three precursors. Toluene, that is, methylbenzene, has a specific gravity of 0.86 and is poorly soluble in water. Acetone, that is, dimethyl ketone, boils at 56.3 °C and is miscible with water in any proportion. Acetic acid anhydride is a mobile, colourless liquid; it has a strong suffocating odour, and the permissible content in air is 3 mg/m3.

Characteristics of toluene. Toluene, that is, methylbenzene, is a clear, colourless liquid with a characteristic odour. Specific gravity 0.86; poorly soluble in water, well miscible with organic solvents. Petrol contains up to 5% toluene; it occupies the main place in pollution of atmospheric air and in toxic effects on human organs.

Uses of toluene. It is used in household chemical industry products: paints, varnishes, adhesive film, chemical cleaning agents and glue synthesis. It is also used in the synthesis of trinitrotoluene and other chemical substances. In the list of precursors, toluene is indicated as a solvent in preparing many narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.

t: Detection of toluene: nitro compound reaction
n: Detection of toluene: nitro compound reaction. When toluene is heated for a long time with conc. sulphuric acid and ammonium nitrate, a nitro compound forms. The mixture begins to give off the smell of bitter almond. Nitro compounds are coloured bluish-violet in acetone and alcoholic NaOH solution.

Properties of acetone. Acetone, that is, dimethyl ketone, is obtained by dry distillation of wood and coal. Chemically pure acetone is a colourless, clear liquid with a characteristic odour; it boils at 56.3 °C and is lighter than water. It is miscible in any proportion with water and organic solvents, for example ether and chloroform. When saturated with table salt, CaCl2 or K2CO3, it separates into two layers. It distils well from mixtures with steam.

Uses of acetone. Acetone is a universal organic solvent: it is used in the production of paints, nitrocellulose, smokeless powder and artificial silk, and in dry cleaning. In pharmacy it serves as raw material in the synthesis of preparations such as chloroform, sulfonal and iodoform; it is also necessary for obtaining synthetic rubber. In addition, acetone as a precursor is also used in the illicit production of narcotic substances.

The iodoform reaction of acetone. Acetone, like ethyl alcohol, readily reacts with an alkaline iodine solution to give iodoform. First NaOI forms from iodine and NaOH; it acts on acetone to give CI3-CO-CH3, and under the action of NaOH iodoform CHI3 is released. The reaction is very sensitive but not characteristic of acetone: substances such as ethyl alcohol and lactic acid also give this reaction.

The nitroprusside and furfural reactions of acetone. With sodium nitroprusside Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] in the presence of alkali, a red-violet colour forms; this reaction is not characteristic of acetone. It is interfered with by acetaldehyde, methyl ethyl ketone, acetophenone, acetylacetone and diacetyl. If an alcoholic solution of furfural, vanillin or salicylaldehyde and alkali are added, then concentrated HCl, a red colour forms when acetone is present.

The reaction of acetone with o-nitrobenzaldehyde. When a solution of o-nitrobenzaldehyde in 2 N alkali is added, a blue colour, that is, indigo, appears if acetone is present. If acetone is scarce, the reaction proceeds slowly: first yellow, then yellow-green and green-blue are observed. Indigo dissolves well in chloroform, so the organic layer is coloured blue.

We compare the qualitative reactions of acetone. The iodoform and sodium nitroprusside reactions are not characteristic of acetone, since other substances also give them. In the furfural reaction a red colour forms if acetone is present, and with o-nitrobenzaldehyde a blue colour, that is, indigo. Acetone is identified by GLC from retention parameters.

Acetone is identified by GLC, on a chromatograph with a flame ionisation detector, from retention parameters. The amount of acetone is also determined by GLC. Remember: acetone is included in the list of precursors.

Characteristics of acetic acid anhydride. It, that is, Acetic anhydride, is a mobile, colourless liquid; it has a strong suffocating odour reminiscent of acetic acid. It dissolves well in benzene, chloroform and ethyl alcohol; the permissible content in air is 3 mg/m3. It is very widely used in the synthesis of organic substances, and is also used in the analysis of many narcotic drugs. It is highly corrosive; the vapours irritate the eyes, nose and throat.

Detection of acetic anhydride. Under the action of water and atmospheric moisture, acetic acid anhydride is hydrolysed to acetic acid. Qualitative reactions characteristic of the acetic acid formed are carried out. If iron (III) chloride is added to the neutralised residue, a red product forms, which turns brown on heating; the sensitivity is 0.5 mg.

t: Acetic anhydride: other reactions and assay
n: Other reactions of acetic acid. If lanthanum nitrate, alcoholic iodine solution and ammonia are added to the residue, a dark blue colour or precipitate forms. When heated with calcium salts, acetone forms, from which indigo can be obtained. With ethyl alcohol and conc. H2SO4, ethyl acetate appears. The amount of acetic acid is determined by the neutralisation method.

Potassium permanganate KMnO4 is a shiny crystalline powder of violet colour; a strong oxidising agent. In medicine it is used as a disinfectant, and it is also used in obtaining narcotic drugs. Its identity is determined by oxidation-reduction reactions: in the presence of sulphuric acid, hydrogen peroxide decolourises the solution.

The amount of potassium permanganate is determined by the iodometric method. Potassium iodide is added to an exact amount of KMnO4 in an acidic medium, whereby an equivalent amount of free iodine is liberated. The iodine is titrated with 0.1 N sodium thiosulphate solution; the indicator is starch.

Sulphuric acid is used as a reagent in obtaining narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. With the addition of barium salts it forms a white precipitate. With the addition of lead salts a white precipitate, that is, lead sulphate, forms; it dissolves in ammonium acetate and caustic alkalis. The amount of sulphuric acid is determined by the neutralisation method.

t: Sulphuric acid: toxicity and rhodizonate (malaka No. 071)
n: Toxicity of sulphuric acid. Sulphuric acid is poisonous to the body; the lethal dose, LD, is given as 5-10 g. Red barium rhodizonate is decolourised by the action of sulphuric acid. In poisoning with the concentrated acid, severe pain, vomiting of blood and convulsions are observed; later perforation of the abdominal cavity is possible.

Hydrochloric acid is also used as a reagent in obtaining narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. In an acidic medium it forms a white precipitate, AgCl, with silver nitrate. When Berthollet salt is added, free chlorine is liberated; if potassium iodide and starch are added, the mixture turns blue. The amount of hydrochloric acid is determined by the neutralisation method.

t: Next lesson: ergot alkaloids, anthranilic acid
n: The topic of the next lesson: ergot alkaloids and anthranilic acid. Ergotamine, ergometrine, lysergic acid and anthranilic acid, which are on the list of precursors, are the principal substances in obtaining narcotic drugs. Ergotamine, ergometrine and lysergic acid are used in obtaining the hallucinogen LSD. Anthranilic acid, in turn, is the principal substance in the synthesis of 4-methylaminorex and methaqualones.

The summary table on identification. For toluene, the nitro compound formation reaction. For acetone, the iodoform, nitroprusside and furfural reactions. For acetic anhydride, hydrolysis, and the FeCl3 and La(NO3)3 reactions. KMnO4 is decolourised by H2O2. H2SO4 gives a white precipitate with barium and lead salts. For HCl, AgNO3 and Berthollet salt are used.

Assay methods. The amount of toluene is determined by GLC and HPLC, that of acetone by GLC. The amounts of acetic, sulphuric and hydrochloric acids are determined by the neutralisation method. For KMnO4, KI is added in an acidic medium and the iodine liberated is titrated with 0.1 N sodium thiosulphate; the indicator is starch.

The reaction of hydrochloric acid with Berthollet salt. When Berthollet salt, KClO3, is added to hydrochloric acid, free chlorine is released. The chlorine formed turns potassium iodide and starch blue. The amount of hydrochloric acid is determined by the neutralisation method.

Conclusion and review questions. Precursors are controlled substances used for preparing narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances; the list has 26 entries. Toluene is identified by the nitro compound reaction; acetone by the iodoform, nitroprusside, furfural and o-nitrobenzaldehyde reactions and by GLC; the anhydride by the FeCl3, La(NO3)3 and ethyl acetate reactions. KMnO4 is decolourised by H2O2 and titrated iodometrically. H2SO4 is identified with barium and lead salts, and HCl with silver nitrate and Berthollet salt.
